strengths: Significance: Reference-based identification of personal objects is a useful robotics problem. VAP provides a practical interface between instance recognition and an existing manipulation policy, without requiring per-object robot demonstrations or policy updates.

Soundness: The proposed pipeline is coherent and the reported improvements are substantial. On the WidowX owl task, VAP achieves 95.0% success versus 62.5% for soft prompting; real-world average success improves from 30.0% to 80.0% for selection and from 18.8% to 56.2% for pick-and-place. Evaluation across four embodiments provides meaningful evidence of practical utility.

Presentation and reproducibility: The grounding, reference voting, tracking, and instruction rewriting are clearly described. Appendix A documents generic policy adaptation and explicitly separates its training objects from evaluation objects. The runtime breakdown also helps assess deployment cost.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript candidly discusses short-horizon scope, grounding errors, cross-view inconsistency, and manipulation failures. Appendix E recognizes privacy and user control over stored references. I find no material ethical concern in the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—missing controlled comparisons: There are no component ablations separating instance retrieval, highlighting, instruction rewriting, and tracking. Crucially, no baseline uses the same retrieved target with another policy interface, such as a bounding-box marker or a grounded spatial description. Thus, the experiments establish that the complete pipeline beats the selected language baselines, but do not establish the specific advantage of the proposed visual prompting design. Oracle-mask evaluation would also clarify the remaining gap between grounding and control.

Soundness—internally inconsistent evaluation reporting: Table 6 reports a 37.6% Fractal failure rate, implying 62.4% success, although every VAP success rate in Table 2 is between 58.2% and 60.6%; no weighted average of those entries can produce 62.4%. Personalized-VLABench is described as 50 episodes per task in Section 4.1, but Table 4 specifies 10 runs of 25 episodes per task. These discrepancies require reconciliation before the aggregate results and error analysis can be trusted.

Statistical support and generalization: Tables report point estimates without uncertainty despite repeated simulation runs, and physical evaluation uses only 20 trials per task. Several gains are modest, such as 60.6% versus 58.8% on the Google Robot bottle task. Each real-world category has one designated personal target and two distractors, without reported rotation of target identity. Repeated placements therefore provide less evidence of generalization to new personal identities than the episode count suggests. Evaluation also remains within the closely related π0/π0.5 policy family.

Originality: The method combines established open-vocabulary detection, DINOv2 matching, SAM2 tracking, and colored visual prompting. This integration can be useful, but the paper does not experimentally distinguish its contribution from the grounded visual-prompting approaches discussed in Section 2. Without matched alternatives or ablations, the new methodological understanding beyond this application remains limited.

Baseline interpretation: The soft-prompt baseline transfers tokens optimized for VLM recognition into a VLA. High recognition accuracy and similar input embedding matrices do not establish that the downstream action expert can use those tokens effectively. Appendix B acknowledges this disconnect, so its failure supports a conclusion about this particular transfer strategy rather than token-based personalization generally. Moreover, hard prompting uses one canonical reference image whereas VAP uses multiple views, leaving unequal reference coverage as a confound.

Reproducibility and presentation: Important settings are unspecified, including tint opacity and color selection, perception-model variants and thresholds, reference-vote tie handling, and policy fine-tuning learning rates. The new benchmarks lack a stated release location or sufficiently detailed asset and reference manifests. Appendix A.3 also reverses the short/long description prompt headings. These omissions matter because both the benchmark construction and the visual intervention are central contributions.

strengths: Significance: Reference-based manipulation of personal objects is a useful problem. VAP offers a practical interface to frozen policies: retrieve the target, track its mask, tint it, and rewrite the instruction. Personalization requires no per-object policy training; the separate environment-adaptation training is disclosed.

Empirical merit: Improvements are substantial across several settings. On WidowX, VAP achieves 95.0% success on owl placement versus 62.5% for the strongest baseline (Table 3). Real-world average success increases from 30.0% to 80.0% for selection and from 18.8% to 56.2% for pick-and-place (Figure 5). Multiple embodiments and physical experiments strengthen the practical contribution.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline is understandable, and the appendix provides adaptation-data descriptions, baseline prompts, and extensive qualitative examples. The discussion candidly addresses cross-view inconsistency, perception failures, and short-horizon scope. Appendix E acknowledges privacy and user control over stored references; no material ethical violation is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—insufficient isolation of the contribution: There are no component ablations or comparisons using the same retrieved target with alternative conditioning, such as a box, crop, or spatial instruction. Nor are there highlight-only, rewrite-only, tracking, or oracle-mask controls. Consequently, the experiments support the complete pipeline against the chosen baselines, but do not establish why its particular visual prompting design is effective or preferable. Quantitative grounding accuracy would also help separate recognition from control.

Evaluation consistency: Section 4.1 reports 50 episodes per VLABench task, whereas Table 4 reports 10 runs of 25 episodes per task and Table 9 reports 1,250 total episodes. More seriously, the Fractal failure rate of 37.6% in Tables 6/9 implies 62.4% success, exceeding every corresponding VAP success rate in Table 2 (58.2–60.6%). These discrepancies need reconciliation. No confidence intervals or variability across the reported runs are provided, limiting interpretation of smaller gains.

Originality and comparative evidence: The methodological novelty is primarily the integration of established detection, embedding retrieval, segmentation/tracking, and visual prompting. This integration can be useful, but the paper needs stronger evidence of the additional understanding it contributes relative to the grounded visual-prompting approaches discussed in Section 2. The soft-prompt baseline receives favorable hard negatives, but embedding-matrix similarity and VQA recognition do not establish that transferred tokens retain their functional meaning for the action expert. Its failure therefore supports a narrower conclusion than a general limitation of token-based personalization.

Significance and generalization: The benchmarks use a small collection of designated targets, with one personal target and two distractors per real-world category. Repeated episodes largely vary configurations rather than personal identity. Swapping which instance is designated personal, evaluating more identities per category, and varying reference quality and distractor similarity would better test personalization. VLABench measures touching rather than grasping or placement, and both policy backbones belong to the π family, further limiting the breadth of demonstrated transfer.

Reproducibility: Important implementation details remain unspecified, including tint values and opacity, their selection procedure, exact perception-model variants and detection thresholds, and handling of retrieval ties or absent targets in individual views. Appendix A.2 gives several training settings but omits the learning rate and schedule. The manuscript also provides no release location for the new benchmark assets, reference sets, or implementation. Together with the inconsistent evaluation counts, these omissions hinder reliable reproduction. Overall, the promising empirical gains warrant further development, but stronger controls and a reproducible, internally consistent evaluation are needed before acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Reference-based selection of personal objects is a useful robotics problem. VAP offers a practical way to connect instance recognition to existing manipulation skills without per-object policy training.

Soundness: The reported improvements span two simulation benchmarks, four robot platforms, and physical experiments. Particularly compelling are WidowX placement results and real-world gains from 30.0% to 80.0% for selection and 18.8% to 56.2% for pick-and-place.

Originality: The contribution is a useful integration of reference-image matching, tracking, and instruction-aligned visual highlighting for frozen VLAs. Its value lies primarily in this application and evaluation rather than new perception algorithms.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline is clearly explained, and the appendix documents backbone adaptation and baseline construction. The discussion candidly acknowledges grounding errors, cross-view inconsistency, and short-horizon scope. Appendix E appropriately recognizes privacy and user control over stored references; no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: There are no component ablations or comparisons that hold grounding fixed. Comparing the same retrieved target communicated through spatial language, bounding boxes, or other visual prompts would establish whether the proposed highlighting interface provides a distinctive benefit. Highlight-only, rewrite-only, oracle-mask, and tracking ablations are also absent. Current results support the complete pipeline over the selected baselines but provide limited understanding of why it works.

Evaluation reporting contains material inconsistencies. Section 4 and Table 1 specify 250 Personalized-VLABench episodes, whereas Table 4 and Table 9 imply 1,250. More importantly, Tables 6 and 9 report 37.6% Fractal failure, implying 62.4% success, although every VAP success rate in Table 2 is at most 60.6%. These figures cannot describe the same pooled evaluation without further explanation.

Statistical reliability is insufficiently documented. Despite repeated simulation runs, no variability or confidence intervals are reported. Physical evaluation uses only 20 trials per task, and some simulation improvements are modest, such as 60.6% versus 58.8% on the bottle task. Paired evaluation protocols and uncertainty estimates are needed to assess these smaller gains.

Reproducibility: Important operational details are missing, including tint opacity, exact perception-model variants and thresholds, retrieval tie handling, and behavior when detections are missing or the target is invisible. Appendix A omits the backbone fine-tuning learning rate. The manuscript provides no artifact link for its new benchmarks, reference sets, or adapted checkpoints.

Scope and baseline interpretation: Evaluation uses a small fixed collection of target identities, including one designated personal instance per real-world category, and only the related π0/π0.5 policy family. This limits evidence for broad instance and backbone generalization. Furthermore, preserved vocabulary embeddings and qualitative attention maps do not establish that VLM-trained soft tokens retain their meaning for the VLA action expert, so their weaker performance does not establish a general limitation of token-based personalization.

strengths: Soundness: The central empirical claim—that reference-based grounding coupled with color highlighting and instruction rewriting improves personalized manipulation—is supported across simulation and physical hardware. Examples include pen-holder success improving from 8.5% to 60.3% (Table 2), and real-world average success improving from 30.0% to 80.0% for selection and 18.8% to 58.8% for pick-and-place (Figure 5). Methods share the same policy backbone within each setting.

Significance: Personal-object disambiguation is a useful robotics problem. The adapter enables registration from a few reference images without per-object policy training. Evaluation spans four robot platforms, selection and manipulation tasks, and single- and multi-camera observations.

Originality: Although the perception components and visual prompting are established techniques, their combination provides a practical interface between instance recognition and frozen action policies. Appendix E supplies useful evidence that aligned visual and language modifications matter: mask-only prompting performs poorly, while the combined intervention substantially improves success.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline is clearly explained, including reference voting, tracking, instruction templates, and fallback behavior. The manuscript distinguishes environment adaptation from per-object training and openly analyzes grounding, cross-view inconsistency, and execution failures. The disclosed use of deployment distractors strengthens the token baseline rather than concealing an evaluation advantage for VAP. I identify no material research-ethics concern in the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Comparative evidence does not fully isolate the value of the proposed interface. The main competitors lack VAP's explicit scene grounding and temporal tracking. A baseline using the same retrieved target and tracker but communicating its location through spatial language or another established visual-prompt interface would better separate recognition gains from prompting gains. The bounding-box ablation is helpful but does not resolve this broader comparison; claims that explicit masks are necessary are consequently too strong.

Generalization is narrower than the framing suggests. The described benchmarks use a small collection of designated personal instances, including one target and two distractors per real-world category, and both policy backbones belong to the same model family. Repeated rollouts establish performance on these objects but do not establish robustness across many unseen identities, reference-image acquisition conditions, or unrelated VLA architectures. Visually indistinguishable objects, target absence, and conflicts between the tint color and existing scene colors are not systematically evaluated.

Statistical reporting limits confidence in smaller improvements. Tables 3 and 4 report means over ten runs without dispersion or confidence intervals; Figure 5's error bars measure variation across tasks rather than uncertainty across trials. Thus, the large main gains are persuasive, but small differences such as voting versus averaging are not established convincingly. Evaluation counts also conflict: Table 9 lists 125 × 10 VLABench episodes, whereas Table 4 implies 250 × 10.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite substantial appendix detail. Exact perception checkpoint variants, detection thresholds, policy learning-rate settings, asset identifiers, reference sets, and precise success criteria for the modified selection tasks are not adequately specified. No release location for the custom benchmarks, adaptation data, or adapted checkpoints is provided.

The token-transfer analysis supports embedding compatibility, not preservation of learned concept behavior through the full VLA. Similar vocabulary embeddings and selected attention visualizations cannot establish that the adapted single-token baseline is representative of stronger token-based personalization methods. Its weakness should therefore be interpreted as a result for this particular implementation.

Some interpretations exceed the measurements. Correct masks followed by failure do not uniquely identify limitations of the underlying policy, because highlighting itself can disrupt control-relevant appearance. Similarly, the reported 20 ms tracking overhead lacks a clear accounting of camera count and execution scheduling, limiting the generality of the real-time claim. These issues qualify an otherwise useful, empirically supported contribution.

strengths: Soundness: The experiments support the central, bounded claim that reference-based grounding plus aligned visual and language prompts can improve frozen-policy manipulation. Gains are substantial: pen-holder success increases from 8.5% to 60.3% (Table 2), and real-world pick-and-place success increases from 18.8% to 58.8% (Figure 5). Policies are shared across methods, and environment-adaptation data exclude evaluation objects.

The component ablations are informative. Table 10 demonstrates that highlighting and instruction rewriting work substantially better together; Table 13 compares mask and box prompts; Tables 11–12 examine reference aggregation and reference count. These provide evidence beyond comparisons with an ungrounded generic policy.

Significance and originality: The method is a modest but useful integration of existing perception and prompting tools. Demonstrating that instance recognition can be translated into executable conditioning without per-object policy updates is practically valuable, and evaluation across four robot platforms strengthens that contribution.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline is clearly explained, with extensive qualitative examples and implementation details. The discussion candidly identifies cross-view inconsistency and residual control failures. These acknowledged limitations appropriately delimit the contribution. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the reported experiments.
weaknesses: The comparison does not fully isolate the advantage of the proposed interface over alternative uses of the same grounding. Hard prompts describe reference images without access to the detected target's scene location. A baseline using identical retrieval followed by spatial language, cropping, or another established grounded prompting interface would be more decisive. The box-prompt ablation helps, but comparisons with the robotics visual-prompting methods cited in Section 2 remain missing.

The soft-token results support conclusions about this particular transfer baseline, not token learning generally. Tokens are trained for recognition in PaliGemma and copied into a VLA. Similar input embeddings and qualitative attention maps do not establish preservation of their downstream meaning through the adapted transformer and action expert. The favorable hard-negative supervision does not resolve this transfer issue.

Benchmark breadth is stronger across embodiments than across personal identities. The real-world benchmark uses one designated target and two distractors per category; repeated placements do not establish generalization across many independently sampled target identities. Figure 2 also includes visibly different colors and shapes, leaving the motivating claims about subtle instance differences insufficiently tested. Both policy backbones belong to the same family.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix. Exact perception checkpoints and thresholds, adaptation learning rates, asset identifiers, and operational success criteria for the customized selection tasks are not specified sufficiently. Episode accounting is inconsistent: Table 4 describes 10 runs of 50 episodes per task, whereas Table 9 lists 125 × 10 total VLABench episodes.

Uncertainty and some interpretations need correction. Simulation tables report means without variability, and Figure 5's error bars measure variation across tasks rather than uncertainty across trials. Small improvements such as voting's 0.4-point Google Robot SR gain are therefore inconclusive. Section 5.4 also says VAP closes the CMR–SR gap, although the absolute real-world gap increases from approximately 11.2 to 13.7 points. The large headline gains remain persuasive, but these stronger statements are not established.

strengths: Soundness: The central empirical claim is supported by substantial gains across simulation and physical hardware using shared frozen policies. On Google Robot visual matching, pen-holder success increases from 8.5% to 60.3% (Table 2). Real-world selection improves from 30.0% to 80.0%, and pick-and-place from 18.8% to 58.8% (Figure 5). These results provide convincing evidence that the adapter helps within the evaluated settings.

Significance: Registering personal objects from a few reference images without per-object policy training addresses a useful deployment problem. Evaluation spans four robot platforms, selection and manipulation tasks, and visual perturbations, providing broader evidence than a single demonstration.

Originality: The contribution is primarily an effective integration and empirical insight: reference-based instance recognition can be translated into familiar color-language cues for a frozen action policy. Appendix E meaningfully supports this design through mask/rewrite ablations, reference-count experiments, and comparisons against bounding-box prompts.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline is clearly explained, including retrieval voting, tracking, instruction rewriting, and fallback behavior. The manuscript explicitly distinguishes environment adaptation from per-object training and candidly discusses cross-view inconsistency and control failures. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the reported tabletop experiments; future privacy concerns are acknowledged.
weaknesses: Comparative evidence: Most baselines lack VAP's explicit scene-level retrieval and tracking. The bounding-box ablation is useful, but a baseline using the same grounding pipeline to generate spatial or relational language would better isolate the benefit of pixel recoloring. Moreover, high VQA accuracy and similar input embedding matrices do not establish that VLM-trained soft tokens retain their meaning through the VLA's modified downstream computation. The comparison supports superiority over this particular transfer recipe, rather than token-based personalization generally.

Generality and significance: The object inventory is small, apparently with one designated personal target per category, and only the closely related π0/π0.5 policy family is tested. Numerous randomized episodes do not substitute for independent target identities. The benchmarks therefore establish useful tabletop instance selection, but provide limited evidence for subtle instance differences, broader policy compatibility, or robust personalization across users. Cross-view inconsistency accounts for roughly half or more of multi-view failures.

Statistical reporting and consistency: Tables 3–4 report means over ten runs without variability, while Figure 5's error bars describe variation across tasks rather than trial uncertainty. This particularly limits interpretation of small ablation gains. Episode counts also conflict: Table 4 specifies five tasks with 50 episodes per run, whereas Table 9 lists 125 × 10 for Personalized-VLABench. The real-world failure rate of 31.9% in Table 6 does not match the approximately 30.6% implied by Figure 5's equally weighted task results.

Reproducibility: Although the appendix provides substantial procedural detail, it does not identify an accompanying code/data release, exact asset inventory and reference sets, perception checkpoint variants and thresholds, or the environment-adaptation learning rate. Success tolerances for the modified selection tasks and physical evaluations also need clearer operational definitions. These omissions make exact benchmark reconstruction difficult.

Claim calibration: Describing the method as an approximation to success-maximizing input optimization is not substantiated by an optimization objective or derivation. Likewise, attention visualizations are suggestive rather than causal evidence about the soft-token failure mechanism. The practical method and large end-to-end improvements justify weak acceptance, but these stronger interpretations and the evaluation gaps prevent a full accept recommendation.
